The positive cells (accent) form one block per triangle plus C–D at 0.4; pairs across the triangles, such as C and E at -0.4, and the diagonal are negative." width="100%"} The modularity matrix compares the actual edges with those expected at random given the degrees: `B = A - k kᵀ / 2m` on an undirected graph, where `k` holds the degrees and `m` is the number of edges (Newman, 2006). Positive entries mark pairs that are more connected than chance. The modularity of a partition is a sum over `B` (see `modularity()`), and its leading eigenvector splits the graph into two communities, the basis of the leading-eigenvector method (`cmty_l_eigenvec()`). On a directed graph this is the Leicht-Newman matrix `A - k_out k_inᵀ / m`. Matches NetworkX's `modularity_matrix()` / `directed_modularity_matrix()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[list[list[float]], list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(matrix, node_ids)`: the matrix as a list of rows, and the node IDs labelling rows and columns, in increasing order. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every row of the undirected modularity matrix sums to zero: ::: {#abbda673 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec matrix, nodes = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(4).modularity_matrix() [[round(v, 3) for v in row] for row in matrix] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[-0.167, 0.667, -0.333, -0.167], [0.667, -0.667, 0.333, -0.333], [-0.333, 0.333, -0.667, 0.667], [-0.167, -0.333, 0.667, -0.167]] ``` ::: :::
